leads.text: Shape-A sweep over scan 2dcd0334453a25e98e0fcdd6682c6d33728872be found NO genuine code_exec/SQL/redirect vulnerability. All 68 precomputed CandidateFlow entries (66 'code_exec', 2 'sql') are mislabeled false positives on manual inspection: the 'code_exec' ones are JsonArrayBuilderImpl/JsonObjectBuilderImpl.validateValue(), JsonGeneratorImpl.writeValue(), System.out.print/println in demo main()s, and JsonPointerImpl's own private helper method named 'execute' (RFC-6901 pointer add/replace/remove on in-memory JSON, not OS exec) — the categorizer appears to pattern-match on the substring 'exec' in method names. The 2 'sql' entries are both the same statement 'String q = req.getQueryString()' in ArrayServlet.java:55, mislabeled because 'getQueryString' contains 'query'; that value is only ever compared with q.equals("stream") and never reaches a database call. A direct graph search for real sink names/text (exec, eval, redirect, Statement, Process, Runtime.exec, executeQuery/Update, prepareStatement, sendRedirect) across the whole scan returned zero genuine OS-command, SQL, or HTTP-redirect sinks, and the declared Dependencies contain no DB driver or process-exec library (only jakarta.json/servlet/ws.rs/xml.bind + JUnit/Hamcrest) — consistent with this scan being the Eclipse Parsson JSON-P library plus its demo apps, which has no such attack surface. No credible code_exec/sql/redirect lead to report.
leads.evidence: MATCH (cf:CandidateFlow {scan_id:$scan_id}) RETURN cf.rank, cf.sink_category, cf.source_uid, cf.sink_uid, cf.path_uids ORDER BY cf.rank -> 68 rows, categories {code_exec:66, sql:2}, all but one a self-loop (source_uid==sink_uid). Pulled CpgCall.code/file_path/line for every uid: code_exec hits resolve to validateValue()/writeValue()/println()/arraycopy()/JsonPointerImpl.execute() (internal helper) — none are OS command execution. The 2 'sql' hits both resolve to 'String q = req.getQueryString()' in demos/servlet/.../ArrayServlet.java:55; follow-up query of all CpgCall in that file shows q is only used in 'q != null && q.equals("stream")' (line 56), never in a DB/query call. Separate query: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.name IN ['exec','system','spawn','eval','Runtime','getRuntime','ProcessBuilder','executeQuery','executeUpdate','prepareStatement','createStatement','sendRedirect','redirect'] OR c.code CONTAINS 'Runtime.getRuntime' OR ... -> 0 rows. Broader toLower(name) CONTAINS 'exec'/'eval'/'redirect'/'statement'/'process' OR toLower(code) CONTAINS 'runtime' -> only JsonPointerImpl.execute(), RuntimeException allocations, and 'execute(NodeReference::add,...)' style internal calls. Dependency check: MATCH (d:Dependency {scan_id:$scan_id}) RETURN d.name,d.version -> hamcrest-core, jakarta.annotation-api, jakarta.json(-api), jakarta.servlet-api, jakarta.ws.rs-api, jakarta.xml.bind-api, jaxb-impl, junit, parsson, parsson-media (no SQL/DB/process libs).

leads.text: Low-severity log-injection candidate: the JAX-RS doPost handlers of ArrayResource, ObjectResource and StructureResource in the demos/rest module take the raw HTTP POST body (a JsonArray/JsonObject/JsonStructure bound to the method parameter 'structure', fully attacker-controlled) and write it straight to the server's standard-output log via System.out.println(structure) with no sanitization, escaping, or rate limiting — the single call inside each doPost's CONTAINS_CALL set is that println. This is CWE-117 (log injection/forging): an attacker can embed newlines/ANSI escape sequences/fake log lines in the JSON string values of the POST body and have them written verbatim into application logs. This is a demo app and the sink is 'log', not one of the primary code_exec/sql/redirect categories, so impact is minor, but it is a real, grounded attacker-input-to-sink flow worth noting.
leads.evidence: MATCH (m:CpgMethod {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE m.full_name CONTAINS 'ArrayResource.doPost' MATCH (m)-[:CONTAINS_CALL]->(c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) RETURN c.uid,c.name,c.code,c.line -> only 2 calls in the method body: System.out.println(structure) and the System.out field access, at ArrayResource.java:42. Parameter query: MATCH (p:CpgParameter {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE p.name='structure' RETURN p.uid,p.name,p.index -> 4 matches at index 1 (the doPost(..., JsonArray/JsonObject/JsonStructure structure) parameter across ArrayResource/ObjectResource/StructureResource). Direct file dump: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path CONTAINS 'ObjectResource.java' ... c.line=53 -> System.out.println(structure); same pattern at StructureResource.java:52 and ArrayResource.java:42 (c.reachable_from_entry=true for all, since ArrayResource.doPost/ObjectResource.doPost/StructureResource.doPost are listed as :EntryPoint handler methods in the ENTERS_AT query).

leads.text: ParserResource.doGet() is a JAX-RS endpoint annotated @Produces("text/html") that streams writeFlickerFeed()'s output directly to the browser. That method builds the entire HTML document ("..." and an tag) by raw string concatenation of 'id', 'farm', 'server', 'secret' fields parsed straight out of a remote JSON feed, with zero HTML-escaping/encoding call anywhere in the method or available in the codebase (no HTML escape/encode/sanitize utility exists in this repo at all -- only JSON-string escaping (writeEscapedString), URL-encoding (Twitter demo), and JSON-pointer encoding were found). If the upstream Flickr response is ever attacker-influenced or MITM'd, those fields are reflected into the HTML response completely unescaped -- the standard output-escaping control is absent.
leads.evidence: Queried CpgMethod for ParserResource.java -> doGet() at line 42 confirmed via semantic_search source: '@GET @Produces("text/html") public StreamingOutput doGet()'. Queried CONTAINS_CALL calls of ParserResource.writeFlickerFeed:void(java.io.OutputStream) -> shows ps.println("") (line 61) and ps.println("") (line 74) built via .addition string concatenation of parser.getString() values, no escape/encode call in that call list. Separately ran: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.name CONTAINS 'escape' OR c.name CONTAINS 'encode' OR c.name CONTAINS 'sanitiz' -> only 13 hits total across the whole repo, all JSON/URL/JsonPointer encoding, none HTML-related; and MATCH (d:Dependency) WHERE name contains 'encoder'/'owasp'/'security'/'escape' -> 0 rows, confirming no escaping utility is even available.

leads.text: In the same ParserResource.writeFlickerFeed(), the outbound request to Flickr's API is made over plain HTTP (http://api.flickr.com/...) rather than HTTPS, and it carries a hardcoded API key (api_key=221160312e1c22ec60ecf336951b0e77) directly in the URL query string in cleartext. There is no transport-encryption control (no https:// anywhere in this request) protecting the credential in transit, so anyone on the network path (including, notably, an attacker who could also tamper with the unencrypted response body that is then reflected unescaped into HTML -- see companion finding) can observe/capture the key.
leads.evidence: Queried CONTAINS_CALL for ParserResource.writeFlickerFeed:void(java.io.OutputStream) -> line 53: 'URL url = new URL("http://api.flickr.com/services/rest/?method=flickr.photos.getRecent&api_key=221160312e1c22ec60ecf336951b0e77&format=json&nojsoncallback=1&per_page=20")' followed by url.openStream() at line 54. Also ran MATCH (c:CpgCall) WHERE c.code CONTAINS 'http://' across the whole scan -> this is the only externally-called http:// URL in the codebase (the Facebook demo and Twitter demo both use https://).

leads.text: TwitterObjectSearch.getSearchStream() builds the OAuth 1.0 request-signing parameter map with a hardcoded, constant 'oauth_nonce' value ("4b25256957d75b6370f33a4501dc5e7e") instead of generating a fresh random/unique nonce per request (there is a '// TODO' comment directly above it, and no SecureRandom/UUID-based nonce generation exists anywhere in the codebase). OAuth 1.0's anti-replay protection depends on each request using a unique nonce; a captured request (e.g. via logs, a proxy, or the same timestamp window) could be replayed against Twitter's API using this code's signature. TwitterStreamSearch.main() reuses this same getSearchStream() method, so the gap is shared by both Twitter demos.
leads.evidence: Queried CONTAINS_CALL for TwitterObjectSearch.getSearchStream:java.io.InputStream() -> line 81 shows the TreeMap literal with comment '// TODO' immediately followed by 'put("oauth_nonce", "4b25256957d75b6370f33a4501dc5e7e")' as a fixed string literal (not derived from any random source). Confirmed via second query MATCH (c:CpgCall) WHERE c.code CONTAINS 'oauth_nonce' OR c.code CONTAINS 'SecureRandom' OR c.code CONTAINS 'UUID' -> only the 3 rows for this same literal TreeMap construction; no SecureRandom/UUID usage exists in the scan. Also confirmed TwitterStreamSearch.java line 44 calls 'TwitterObjectSearch.getSearchStream()' directly, inheriting the same nonce.

leads.text: The demo JAX-RS POST endpoints (ArrayResource.doPost, ObjectResource.doPost, StructureResource.doPost) accept arbitrary JSON structures from any network caller with no authentication or authorization check anywhere on the request path -- no @RolesAllowed/@PermitAll/session/login-check call appears anywhere in the demos/rest module. Current impact is low (the handlers only System.out.println the parsed structure), but the standard access-control control (authn/authz on a state-accepting route) is entirely absent, so if this sample were extended to do anything consequential with the POST body it would be wide open.
leads.evidence: Queried full call lists of ArrayResource.doPost/ObjectResource.doPost/StructureResource.doPost -> bodies only contain 'System.out.println(structure)' with no preceding auth check. Separately ran MATCH (c:CpgCall) WHERE c.code CONTAINS 'login'/'authenticate'/'Authorization'/'RolesAllowed'/'session' across the whole scan -> the only hit in the entire codebase is an outbound 'Authorization' HTTP header set by the Twitter demo client (unrelated); zero authorization checks exist on any of the demos/rest or demos/servlet entry points.

leads.text: In the Twitter demo's OAuth1 request-signing code, the oauth_nonce value is hardcoded to the constant string "4b25256957d75b6370f33a4501dc5e7e" instead of being randomly generated per request, with a bare '// TODO' comment sitting directly above the hardcoded value -- indicating the developer flagged this as incomplete/wrong and never fixed it. A nonce is supposed to be unique per OAuth request to prevent replay attacks; reusing the same nonce for every request defeats that protection. The enclosing method getSearchStream() is reachable from entry (main -> getSearchStream, hop_distance 2) per the precomputed reachability, i.e. it executes on every run of this demo.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall) WHERE c.scan_id=$scan_id AND (toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'todo' OR toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'fixme' OR toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'disable' OR toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'insecure' OR toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'temporar' OR toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'workaround' OR toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'vulnerable' OR toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'hack' OR toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'bypass' OR toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'unsafe' OR toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'deprecated' OR toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'legacy') RETURN c.code, c.file_path, c.line, c.name -- returned 3 rows, all the same TreeMap initializer at demos/twitter/.../TwitterObjectSearch.java:81 containing: 'put("oauth_consumer_key", consumerKey); // TODO put("oauth_nonce", "4b25256957d75b6370f33a4501dc5e7e"); put("oauth_signature_method", "HMAC-SHA1"); ...'. Follow-up substring search for 'oauth_nonce' confirmed this hardcoded nonce is unique to this one site (not present in sibling TwitterStreamSearch.java). Follow-up query on CpgMethod for this file showed getSearchStream (line 67) has reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=2, and main() (line 46) is hop_distance=0, confirming this code path executes on normal program flow from the entry point.

leads.text: Breadth-first sweep found ZERO regex usage anywhere in this codebase (no RegExp/Pattern.compile/matches/.find/.group calls, no code containing 'regex'/'Regex', no literal strings with regex-like syntax such as ^...$ anchors). This is a hand-written char-by-char JSON tokenizer (org.eclipse.parsson.JsonTokenizer) with no regex-based parsing or validation anywhere, so the catastrophic-backtracking (ReDoS) sub-class of Shape D does not apply to this scan -- confirmed empty, not merely unchecked.
leads.evidence: Ran 5 queries across this session filtering on scan_id=2dcd0334453a25e98e0fcdd6682c6d33728872be: (1) CpgCall where code matches regex-literal-like syntax or name='RegExp' or code CONTAINS 'RegExp' -> 0 structural-regex matches (8 unrelated '+'-string-concat hits returned by the loose regex filter, all plain string concatenation, not regex); (2) CpgCall.name IN ['match','test','replace','search','split','exec'] -> 4 hits, all plain String.replace/split (JsonPatchImpl.java, JsonPointerImpl.java), none regex-related; (3) CpgCall.name IN ['matches','compile','find','group','Pattern'] -> 0 rows; (4) CpgCall.code CONTAINS 'Pattern.compile'/'Pattern' -> 0 rows; (5) CpgCall.code CONTAINS '\\d'/'\\w'/'[0-9]'/'regex'/'Regex' -> 0 rows; (6) CpgCall.code CONTAINS '^' AND CONTAINS '$' -> 0 rows; (7) CpgModule nodes (any language) -> 0 rows total; (8) semantic_search for 'regular expression pattern matching validation' returned only unrelated tokenizer/message-formatting code, confirming no regex code chunk exists to retrieve.

leads.text: Dependency manifest for this scan lists 11 third-party components, several with versions old enough or unresolved enough to warrant a manual CVE check as part of the components-with-known-vulnerabilities class (CWE-1104/CWE-937): concrete pinned versions are hamcrest-core 1.3 (released 2012), jakarta.servlet-api 5.0.0, org.glassfish.jaxb:jaxb-impl 3.0.1, and junit 4.13.2; the remaining components (jakarta.annotation-api, jakarta.json, jakarta.json-api, jakarta.ws.rs-api, jakarta.xml.bind-api, parsson, parsson-media) have unresolved Maven property placeholders (e.g. '${jakarta.annotation-api.version}') instead of concrete version strings in this scan's extracted manifest, so their actual shipped versions could not be verified here and should be resolved from the real POM before ruling them in or out. This is a flag-for-review lead, not a confirmed vulnerable-version match: the exploit-reference corpus needed to corroborate specific CVEs against these exact versions was unindexed/unavailable in this session.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (d:Dependency {scan_id:$scan_id}) RETURN d.name, d.version ORDER BY d.name -> 11 rows: hamcrest-core/1.3, jakarta.annotation-api/${jakarta.annotation-api.version}, jakarta.json/${project.version}, jakarta.json-api/${jakarta.json-api.version}, jakarta.servlet-api/5.0.0, jakarta.ws.rs-api/${jakarta.ws.rs-api.version}, jakarta.xml.bind-api/${jakarta.xml.bind-api.version}, jaxb-impl/3.0.1, junit/4.13.2, parsson/${project.version}, parsson-media/${project.version}. Follow-up: mcp__orion__exploit_search for 'jaxb-impl deserialization XXE vulnerability', 'jakarta servlet-api vulnerability', and 'junit hamcrest vulnerability' each returned {"_note":"exploit corpus unavailable: not indexed"} -- so no specific CVE could be corroborated from this session's tools.
